questions.prompt: Walk through the employment-change lifecycle as GlobeHire's domain type encodes it: which states exist and which one a new change starts in, what a change must satisfy to exist at all, which transitions are legal and what guards each one, which states are terminal, and what the employment-change validate endpoint actually does with the type, including where its notion of 'today' comes from. Close with the offboarding checklist's rule.

keyPoints.text: [w3] There are four states (Proposed, Approved, Applied, Cancelled), and a new change starts in Proposed only because the constructor never assigns Status and Proposed is the enum's zero value.
[w3] The constructor is the gate: non-empty ids and change type, an effective date not before today, and a non-blank reason, each refused with its own business-rule code.

[w3] Approve and Apply both go through one Transition helper that demands the exact source state (Proposed to Approved, Approved to Applied), so skipping approval or applying twice fails with transition_invalid.
[w2] Apply has a second guard on top of the state check: it refuses before the effective date (not_effective).
[w2] Cancel works from Proposed or Approved and needs a reason; Applied and Cancelled are terminal, since no method moves a change out of either.

[w3] The validate endpoint only constructs the change and echoes its id and status; nothing is stored, the clientId in the route is never read, and Today comes from the request body, so the caller decides what today is and can satisfy the not-in-the-past rule with any date it likes.
[w1] Offboarding has three required tasks (final pay, access revoked, documents issued); an unknown task is refused and ending employment requires all three.

questions.prompt: Explain GlobeHire's compliance-case gate: what a case requires when it is created, which evidence it accepts and in which state, what moving a case to review checks, what becomes of the case when some evidence has lapsed by then, and what approval requires. Then defend or indict it as a state machine: which moves does it fail to guard, and can a case recover from every state it can reach?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Creation needs an id, a subject reference and at least one non-blank evidence type; the types are trimmed and collected into an ordinal set, so duplicates collapse.

[w3] Evidence is accepted only while the case is collecting evidence, only for a required type and with a reference; already-expired evidence is refused, and recording a type again replaces the earlier evidence for it.
[w2] Moving to review first requires evidence for every required type (evidence_incomplete otherwise).

[w3] If any recorded evidence has expired by the review date, the method sets the case to Expired and then throws: the call fails yet still changes state, so whether Expired sticks depends on what the caller does with the aggregate after the exception.
[w3] Expired is a dead end: evidence can only be recorded while collecting evidence, so a case that expired can never take fresh evidence and never reach review.
[w3] Submitting for review never checks the current state, so calling it on an already Approved case with complete, unexpired evidence demotes it to ReadyForReview.
[w2] Approval is the one properly guarded move: only a ReadyForReview case can be approved (not_ready otherwise).

questions.prompt: Explain how GlobeHire's bulk workforce-plan validation reports failure: what fails the whole request and what fails only a row, the order of the checks a row goes through, how duplicate keys are detected and what that order means for a batch whose first copy of a key is itself invalid, and how a domain failure becomes an HTTP response, with which status and body. Then say which failures fall outside that contract.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Only the batch size fails the whole request: fewer than 1 or more than 1,000 rows throws; otherwise every row gets an outcome.

[w3] Partial failure is returned as data: totals of all, valid and invalid rows plus one outcome per row (row number, external key, valid flag, error code), in a successful response even when every row is invalid.

[w3] A row is checked in a fixed order: identity (row number at least 1, non-blank key), then duplicate key, then country code, then currency and a positive amount; the first failure is the row's only reported code.

[w2] The duplicate check registers a key before the field checks run, so the first copy claims the key even if it then fails on country or currency; a later, otherwise valid row with that key is reported as the duplicate.
[w2] Keys are trimmed but compared ordinally, so the duplicate check is case-sensitive: EMP-1 and emp-1 both pass.

[w3] The exception handler handles only business-rule violations: it logs the code at Information and writes a 422 problem-details body with title, detail, the stable code and the trace id; any other exception is declined and falls through to the framework's generic 500.

[w2] Because the mapping keys on the exception type alone, a stale hire-case version is also a 422, indistinguishable by status from a validation failure; only its code (concurrency.version_mismatch) tells a client or a retrying gateway the difference.
